deep.reconstruction:
Context: E260 models a steady (quasi-steady) outflow of water through a vessel made of cylindrical pieces. The model includes a 'friction' term. Euler takes the friction to be proportional to the local pressure p and to the element of length divided by the width, dr = ds/z. In modern terms it is a Coulomb/Amontons-type wall friction: shear proportional to normal pressure times perimeter over area. The momentum balance along a streamline is a Bernoulli law with an extra term αp dr. It is integrated with the factor e^{αr}: e^{αr}p = C + ∫e^{αr}dx + b^4 v·4∫e^{αr}dz/z^5. Here x is the vertical descent, z² is the section, b² is the orifice section, and v is the height due to the outflow velocity, so the local velocity height is v b^4/z^4.

Previous page: for the first vertical tube (width g, length a), with C = l (atmospheric pressure as a water-column height), the pressure just below the sudden contraction from g to f at F is
l e^{-αa/g} + (g/α)(1 − e^{-αa/g}) + b^4 v(1/g^4 − 1/f^4).

This page:
(§28) For the second tube FD (width f, inclined so dx = ds cos ζ, r = s/f restarted at F), the term 4∫e^{αr}dz/z^5 vanishes in the interior. At the sudden contraction to the orifice CD (z = b, at s = b) it equals e^{αb/f}(1/f^4 − 1/b^4).
(§29) The interior pressure is p = C e^{-αs/f} + (f/α)(1 − e^{-αs/f}) cos ζ. This solves dp = cos ζ ds − αp ds/f. The new constant C equals the pressure at F found above. At the orifice the pressure is C e^{-αb/f} + (f/α)(1 − e^{-αb/f}) cos ζ + b^4 v(1/f^4 − 1/b^4).
(§30) Setting this equal to the atmospheric pressure l and substituting C gives a linear equation in v.
(§31) Solving it gives the efflux height
v = [l(1 − e^{-αa/g − αb/f}) − (g/α)e^{-αb/f}(1 − e^{-αa/g}) − (f/α)(1 − e^{-αb/f}) cos ζ] / [e^{-αb/f} b^4/g^4 + (1 − e^{-αb/f}) b^4/f^4 − 1].

Checks: as α→0 this reduces to v = (a + b cos ζ)/(1 − b^4/g^4), Torricelli's law corrected for the finite vessel. For small α the loss is proportional to α(a/g + b/f)·l, which is why (next page) Euler concludes that atmospheric pressure increases the frictional loss.
errors: Notation clash in the original: b denotes both the half-width of the orifice CD (section b², velocity factor b^4/z^4) and the length of tube FD ('vbi subito est z=b, et s=b'). Formally the algebra is consistent if one reads the s=b as the length, but the same letter cannot be both. This produces confusing expressions on the next page, e.g. αb·b^4/f^5.
Misprint in §31 numerator: the exponent printed as −αa/g − αb/b should be −αa/g − αb/f, as in §30.
Printer's slip: 'Pprodibit' and 'alti- huic' (the syllable '-tudo' of 'altitudo' is dropped at the line break).

Physical (not algebraic) defect: friction is made proportional to absolute pressure, so the predicted head loss depends on atmospheric pressure and would nearly vanish in vacuo. Real pipe friction depends on velocity, not on ambient pressure. The algebra on this page is otherwise correct (verified the ODE solution, the jump terms and the solution for v).

ideas.what: Integrating-factor solution of the pressure ODE along a pipe with pressure-proportional friction, piecewise over cylindrical segments with Bernoulli jumps at sudden contractions
ideas.modern_name: First-order linear ODE / quasi-one-dimensional pipe flow with Coulomb-type wall friction
ideas.where_published: E260, Novi Comment. Acad. Sci. Petrop. 6 (1756/7, publ. 1761)

ideas.what: Frictionless limit giving Torricelli's law with finite-vessel correction v = H/(1 − b^4/g^4)
ideas.where_published: Euler's hydraulic papers of the 1750s; D. Bernoulli 1738

ideas.what: Friction loss scaling with length/width (r = s/f), i.e. inversely with the pipe size, combined with a dependence on ambient pressure
ideas.modern_name: Wall friction proportional to wetted perimeter/area (precursor of the hydraulic-radius dependence of Chézy/Du Buat), but with a Coulomb rather than velocity-dependent law
ideas.usually_credited_to: Chézy (1769/1775), Du Buat (1779) for the hydraulic-radius resistance law
ideas.where_published: E260; whether the Opera omnia II editors (Truesdell's introductions to vols. II.12–13) discuss this page in detail: unsure

missed.claim: Euler's quantitative prediction that pipe-flow friction losses scale with atmospheric pressure is the empirically testable consequence of his pressure-proportional friction law. It is a historical curiosity (a falsifiable but wrong model) rather than a missed result. It is likely noted in the hydraulics histories, but I am unsure of its explicit treatment.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Only historiographical: it marks an early continuum-mechanics attempt at wall friction modelled on solid (Amontons–Coulomb) friction, before velocity-dependent laws.

deep.surprise_reason: Routine algebra completing Euler's published model. The results are correct apart from misprints and a notation clash. The physically dubious pressure-dependent friction is the page's only notable feature, and it is the stated premise of the published paper.
transcription_corrections: In the §31 numerator, the image reads 'αb/b' but the intended exponent is −αa/g − αb/f (a misprint in the original, faithfully transcribed).
'Pprodibit enim alti- huic celeritati debita' is a misprint in the original for 'Prodibit enim altitudo huic celeritati debita'.
In the §28 display, the transcription 'z^5' in the denominator is consistent with the previous page (the image shows z with a superscript, likely 5).
